title: England’s Conquest & the Rise of the British Empire: Full History
author: Glenn Junsay Pansensoy
excerpt: How England built the world’s largest empire through trade, war, and treaties—and the conquest, resistance, and legacy it left behind.
body:
Prologue

At its peak, in the early twentieth century, this one island nation ruled roughly a quarter of the world's land and people. And yet, it was not even the first European empire.

Britain arrives late: navy, finance and industry, 1600s to 1800s

Portugal sailed the Atlantic and Indian Oceans first. Spain, after 1492, built a vast American empire on silver mining, plantations, and forced labor.

Britain arrived late. But it learned from these rivals, competed with them, and eventually surpassed them.

In 1606, King James the First granted charters to the London Company and the Plymouth Company, letting English investors plant settlements in North America.

In 1607, Jamestown in Virginia became one of the first permanent English settlements in the Americas.

The Royal Navy was the empire's backbone. It guarded merchant ships, secured sea lanes, defeated rivals, and carried British force across every ocean.

Behind the ships stood money: banks, insurance, credit, and joint-stock companies, which let investors share the risk of voyages lasting years.

Then came the Industrial Revolution. Factories hungry for cotton, rubber, and tin turned colonies into suppliers, and into markets for British goods.

That loop made empire profitable for Britain, but it often held back industrial development in the societies it ruled.

How the empire ruled: settlers, indirect rule and treaties

Britain ruled in several ways. In North America and Australia, settlers built permanent colonies and displaced Indigenous peoples.

In India and Malaya, it often ruled indirectly, through local rulers, traditional elites, and appointed officials.

And treaties, often signed under military pressure, could transfer territory, open ports, and grant special rights: domination written as diplomacy.

India: from the East India Company to the Raj, 1600s to 1947

Our first case is India. The East India Company arrived in the early seventeenth century as a trading firm, seeking textiles, spices, and indigo, with permission from Mughal rulers.

Over time, the Company gained an army, collected taxes, made treaties, and governed territory. A trading firm had become a state.

In June 1757, at the Battle of Plassey, Company forces under Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah, the Nawab of Bengal, helped by the betrayal of key Bengali commanders.

Plassey did not make Britain master of India overnight, but it gave the Company decisive influence in Bengal.

In 1764, at the Battle of Buxar, the Company defeated a coalition of Indian forces.

In 1765, the Treaty of Allahabad granted the Company the diwani: the right to collect revenue in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.

Now a company could tax millions of people. That revenue paid its soldiers, bought goods for export, and financed still more conquest.

Parliament noticed. The Regulating Act of 1773 and Pitt's India Act of 1784 brought the Company under growing government control.

After the Rebellion of 1857, the Government of India Act and Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 moved power from the Company to the Crown.

The British Raj followed: a Viceroy, the Indian Civil Service, and direct rule, which lasted until independence in 1947.

Railways, telegraphs, and ports spread across India, but largely to serve imperial trade and military needs. Farmers were pushed toward cotton, indigo, and opium.

Meanwhile, cheap British factory textiles competed with Indian handloom weavers, bringing hardship to many regions.

China: the Opium Wars and the unequal treaties, 1839 to 1997

China was never colonized in the same way. It stayed formally independent under the Qing dynasty, but Britain used war and treaties to pry open its markets.

The issue was opium. Merchants shipped opium grown in British India to China, fueling addiction and a deep social and economic crisis.

When the Qing tried to stop the trade, Britain answered with force. The First Opium War ran from 1839 to 1842.

Britain's navy attacked coastal cities and controlled key waterways. On August 29, 1842, the Treaty of Nanjing was signed aboard a British warship.

China ceded Hong Kong Island, opened five ports to foreign trade, and paid a large indemnity. This began the era of the unequal treaties.

More followed: the Treaty of the Bogue in 1843, the Treaty of Tianjin in 1858, and the Convention of Peking in 1860, which ceded Kowloon.

Hong Kong became a major British port and financial center, governed by Britain until 1997.

The Americas: colonies, Indigenous nations and slavery, 1606 to 1833

Back across the Atlantic, British settlement spread from Virginia to New England, the Caribbean, and later Canada. The Mayflower Compact of 1620 sketched a framework for self-government among Plymouth's settlers.

For Indigenous nations, the consequences were severe: disease, warfare, land seizure, and displacement from lands they had inhabited for thousands of years.

The empire also became deeply tied to the transatlantic slave trade. Enslaved Africans were transported to work sugar, tobacco, and cotton plantations.

It generated enormous profit for British merchants, planters, and financial institutions, at immense human cost.

The Royal Proclamation of 1763 reserved lands west of the Appalachians for Indigenous peoples. In practice, settlers and speculators often ignored it.

Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807, and slavery in most colonies in 1833, though with years of forced 'apprenticeship'. A major moral achievement, after centuries of profit.

Australia: the First Fleet and terra nullius, 1770 to 1788

Captain James Cook charted Australia's east coast in 1770. In 1788, the First Fleet reached Port Jackson and founded a penal colony near present-day Sydney.

British authorities treated the land as terra nullius, 'land belonging to no one', denying the sovereignty of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and bypassing any treaty.

The effects were devastating: loss of land, water, and sacred sites, disease, violence, massacres, and forced removals. Their consequences endure today.

Wool, farming, and mining built a settler economy, while Indigenous peoples were shut out of political power.

New Zealand: the Treaty of Waitangi, 1840

New Zealand took a different path. Cook charted its coast in 1769 and 1770, and missionaries, traders, and settlers followed.

In 1840, the Crown and many Māori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi. But the English and Māori versions differed on sovereignty and authority.

Disputes over land led to the New Zealand Wars, and Māori lost vast territories. In 1975, the Waitangi Tribunal was created to hear their grievances.

Malaya: the Pangkor Treaty and indirect rule, 1874

In Malaya, Britain ruled indirectly. The Pangkor Treaty of 1874 placed a British Resident beside the Sultan of Perak, leaving religion and Malay custom to local authorities.

The Residents gradually gained control of finance and administration, and the Federated Malay States of 1895 centralized the colonial structure.

Tin mines and rubber plantations drove exports, with Singapore as the commercial hub. Chinese and Indian labor migration reshaped society, and created lasting divisions.

The economy of empire

Across the empire, cotton, tea, sugar, rubber, tin, opium, and manufactured goods moved along a vast network, enriching British ports, banks, insurers, and shippers.

Joint-stock companies, banks, and commercial law spread worldwide. But colonial economies were largely organized to serve British industry, not local development.

Language, schools and ideas

The English language spread through administration, commerce, schools, law, and print, becoming a major language of diplomacy, science, and business.

Colonial schools trained clerks, lawyers, and teachers, and some of those graduates used the ideas of rights and self-government to challenge British rule.

Culture flowed both ways. Colonized peoples adapted British institutions into new political movements, literatures, and national identities.

Resistance and decolonization, 1857 to 1997

Resistance never stopped: the 1857 rebellion in India, Indigenous war and diplomacy in the Americas, Aboriginal resistance in Australia, Māori challenges in New Zealand, and nationalists in Malaya.

After World War Two, a weakened Britain faced stronger nationalist movements. In 1947, India and Pakistan became independent.

Many former colonies joined the Commonwealth. In 1997, Hong Kong returned to China, often seen as the symbolic end of Britain's territorial empire.

Britain today

Britain still shapes the world through the Commonwealth, the English language, London's financial markets, its universities, and its cultural exports.

And debates over reparations, racism, Indigenous land rights, migration, and how to remember empire continue in Britain and in its former colonies.

Conclusion: power, resistance and inequality

Britain came late. Yet it succeeded by combining commerce, naval strength, finance, industry, and political organization.

Its empire brought trade and institutions, and also conquest, exploitation, and dispossession. It cannot be told only as progress.

It is a story of power, resistance, and inequality, and understanding it helps explain the world we live in. Thank you for watching.
